title: The truth will set you free (John 8:31–59)
carry: the truth shall make you free

segments.voice: Yesterday, golden lamps in the temple, and Jesus saying: I am the light of the world. Your line was the light of life. What was your next step? Day six hundred sixteen.

Some sentences escape their books. Today's has. It's carved in stone in the lobby of the CIA's original headquarters building in Virginia. It's on university buildings and library walls. In Latin, it's the motto of Johns Hopkins University. Politicians quote it, journalists quote it, people who've never opened a Bible quote it. "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Out of context, it sounds like a slogan for information: get the facts, and you'll be free. But in John's Gospel it's the middle of a hard conversation, and the sentence before it changes everything.

Here's the sentence before: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed." Continue means stay, abide, live there. So the truth Jesus means isn't a fact you look up. It's something you come to know by staying close to him, the way you only really know a friend by spending years together. And the freedom he means isn't political. His hearers object: "We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man." Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin. The freedom he offers is from the inside out. The argument gets sharp. Both sides claim Abraham. This chapter contains hard words, spoken in a fierce argument among Jews, and over the centuries some Christians twisted those words into hatred of Jewish people, with terrible results. Churches today, Catholic and Protestant, have taught clearly against that reading. Then comes the line that ends the argument: "Before Abraham was, I am." Not before Abraham was, I was. I am. The same two Greek words as the voice on the water, ego eimi. The tenses don't match, and his listeners hear it as a claim to God's own name. They pick up stones, and he slips away. Look back over this week: bread of life, Peter's to whom shall we go, judging rightly at the feast of booths, belly, a stone set down, light, and now truth that frees.
screen: then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one freeing truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of something true that you've been avoiding saying. An apology you owe. A thank you you've never spoken. A boundary you need. Or just something true about how you feel. Notice how it sits in you, unsaid. Heavy, maybe, or tight. Imagine saying it, simply and kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Notice what loosens. If you pray, you can ask for courage and gentleness. If you don't, simply choose the words you'd use. The bell holds the time.
Truth. Jesus's promise to those who continue in his word: knowing it by staying close, and being freed by it.
Your line: the truth shall make you free. Today, say the true thing you chose, kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day six hundred sixteen, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians read this passage as teaching that freedom comes from staying with Jesus's word; churches today also teach clearly against using John 8 to blame or demean Jewish people.

what a scholar hears: "before Abraham was, I am" sets a past tense against a present one with ego eimi, and this chapter's hard words were later misused against Jews.

notes: John 8:32 is inscribed in the lobby of the CIA's Original Headquarters Building (Langley, Virginia). Confirm.
Johns Hopkins University motto 'Veritas vos liberabit'. Confirm.

The script names the misuse of John 8:44 against Jewish people without quoting it, and says 'many churches today teach clearly against that reading' (e.g., Nostra Aetate, 1965, and many Protestant statements). Confirm phrasing.
'Grammar deliberately broken': 'before Abraham came to be (genesthai), I am (ego eimi)'. Confirm wording.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'some of the hardest words in the Gospels', 'many churches' and 'misused for centuries'; 'grammar deliberately broken' (an intent claim) now 'the tenses don't match'. CIA lobby and Johns Hopkins motto facts kept; confirm.
